title: Debating
why: After the mechanics of the subjunctive, this lesson gives you the words of a real discussion: framing your opinion, agreeing, disagreeing politely and nuancing. It closes the unit on opinions with debates on very French topics: city or countryside, remote work and the long lunch break.

{"lessons": ["

Saying what you think

You now have the grammar of opinion: the indicative after je pense que, the subjunctive after je ne pense pas que. This lesson gives you the words that frame an opinion and link arguments, so you can hold your own in a real discussion: at a dinner, in a meeting, at the coffee machine.

FrenchEnglishNote
À mon avis, …In my opinion, …never \"dans mon opinion\"
Selon moi, … / D'après moi, …As I see it, …also selon toi ?, selon vous ?
Pour moi, …For me, …very common in speech
Personnellement, …Personally, …to set yourself apart
Je trouve que…I think, I find that…a personal impression, + indicative

Être d'accord, avoir raison

Two small words, two classic mistakes. \"I agree\" is built with être: je suis d'accord, never \"j'accorde\". \"You're right\" and \"you're wrong\" are built with avoir, like avoir faim or avoir froid: tu as raison, tu as tort.

— À mon avis, Lyon est plus agréable que Paris. — Je suis d'accord avec toi.— In my opinion, Lyon is nicer than Paris. — I agree with you.
Vous avez raison, c'est trop loin.You're right, it's too far.

À mon avis and selon moi already mean \"I think\": don't add je pense que after them. À mon avis, je pense que… sounds as clumsy as \"In my opinion, I think that…\". Say À mon avis, c'est trop cher, or simply Je pense que c'est trop cher.

", "

Agreeing, disagreeing, nuancing

A good discussion is rarely yes or no. Here is a scale, from full agreement to full disagreement:

FrenchEnglish
Je suis tout à fait d'accord.I completely agree.
Tu as raison. / Vous avez raison.You're right.
Tu as raison, mais…You're right, but…
Il est vrai que…, mais… / C'est vrai que…, mais…It's true that…, but…
Ça dépend.It depends.
Je ne suis pas tout à fait d'accord.I don't completely agree.
Je ne suis pas du tout d'accord.I don't agree at all.
Tu as tort.You're wrong.

Don't mix up pas tout à fait (not completely: polite nuance) and pas du tout (not at all: a clear no). Ça dépend takes de before a noun: ça dépend du travail, ça dépend des gens.

The subjunctive comes back

When you disagree or regret something, the triggers of the last two lessons appear naturally:

Je ne pense pas que ce soit une bonne idée.I don't think it's a good idea.
Je ne suis pas sûr que tout le monde puisse travailler à la maison.I'm not sure everyone can work from home.
C'est dommage que les gens prennent moins le temps de déjeuner.It's a shame people take less time for lunch.

Il est vrai que and c'est vrai que take the indicative: you admit a fact before answering it. C'est vrai que la ville est chère, mais il y a tout.

", "

Linking arguments

To build an argument, you need words that show contrast. French has a richer set than \"but\" and \"however\", and each one has its own nuance:

FrenchEnglishUse
d'un côté… de l'autre…on the one hand… on the other…weighing two sides
pourtantyet, and yeta surprising contrast
cependanthowevermore formal: writing, meetings
en revancheon the other hand, by contrastcomparing two different things
par contreon the other handthe spoken version of en revanche
Il fait très beau. Pourtant, Hugo reste à la maison.It's a beautiful day. And yet Hugo is staying home.
La ville est bruyante. En revanche, tout est près.The city is noisy. On the other hand, everything is close by.
D'un côté, le télétravail évite les trajets ; de l'autre, on voit moins ses collègues.On the one hand, remote work saves commuting; on the other, you see your colleagues less.

A very French topic: the lunch break

In France, la pause déjeuner often lasts an hour, and many people still eat a real meal, sitting down, with colleagues. It's a perfect topic to practice: D'un côté, c'est long ; de l'autre, on mange mieux et on discute.

English often says \"on the other hand\" without \"on the one hand\". In French, use en revanche or par contre for that. On its own, de l'autre côté means \"on the other side\" (of the street, of the river).
